analysis.one_liner: Bans racial profiling by law enforcement and ties federal police grants to anti-profiling policies.
analysis.headline: Backed by 19 Senate Democrats and a December 2014 subcommittee hearing, the bill never reached a Senate vote and died when the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it illegal for any federal, state, local, or tribal law enforcement agent to rely on race, ethnicity, national origin, or religion when deciding whom to stop, search, or investigate. People harmed by profiling could sue for a court order to stop the practice, and federal law enforcement agencies would have to adopt anti-profiling policies and collect data on their stops. State and local police would have to certify they have such policies to keep receiving major federal justice grants, and the Justice Department would publish annual reports on profiling by agency.
analysis.who_benefits: Racial, ethnic, and religious minorities who are disproportionately stopped, searched, and investigated by police — including in traffic stops, pedestrian stops, and immigration and border enforcement. People who can show a department's stops fall heavily on minorities would have a clear right to go to court for injunctive relief, with attorney's fees available if they win. Communities would also get public, agency-by-agency data on who gets stopped and searched.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Minorities targeted by police stops and searches

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits any federal, state, local, or tribal law enforcement agent or agency from engaging in racial profiling, defined as relying to any degree on race, ethnicity, national origin, or religion in deciding whom to stop or investigate.

Lets the United States or an individual injured by racial profiling sue for a court order to end the practice, against the government body, the officer, and any supervisor with authority over that officer; a showing that stops in a jurisdiction fall disparately on minorities counts as initial evidence of a violation.
Requires federal law enforcement agencies to maintain anti-profiling policies, officer training, complaint procedures, and data collection, and to cease existing practices that permit profiling.

Conditions federal justice grants (Edward Byrne Memorial and Cops on the Beat) on state and local agencies certifying they have anti-profiling policies and have eliminated profiling practices, with the Attorney General empowered to withhold funds from agencies that do not comply.

Requires the Justice Department to collect and publish standardized data on stops and searches — including 'hit rates' showing how often searches find contraband — with annual public reports to Congress on disparities, while protecting the identities of officers and individuals in the data.

analysis.who_pays: Law enforcement agencies, primarily. State, local, tribal, and federal agencies would bear the cost of collecting and reporting stop data, changing policies, and training officers, and departments where profiling is found would face lawsuits and court orders. Police departments and local governments risked losing federal Byrne and COPS grant money if they did not certify compliance.
analysis.who_pays_short: Law enforcement agencies and local governments

drawbacks.text: The bill lets a disparate impact — stops that fall unevenly on minority groups — serve as prima facie evidence of a violation, which would expose departments to litigation even where officers never intentionally profiled, and would let suits reach individual officers' supervisors and the employing government.

The profiling ban applies to immigration and customs enforcement, including workplace investigations and enhanced inspections of people entering the country, which border security officials have traditionally argued requires attention to nationality and origin; agencies could also lose Byrne and COPS grant funds if they failed to certify compliance.

Mandatory data collection and reporting on every stop and search nationwide would impose ongoing administrative and technology costs on thousands of federal, state, local, and tribal agencies, though the bill authorizes federal grants to help small and rural departments build data systems.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is straightforward: stronger protection against being stopped or searched because of who you are, in exchange for compliance costs and litigation exposure for police agencies. The private right of action with a disparate-impact evidentiary standard is the most aggressive part and the likeliest source of pushback from law enforcement. The grant conditions use money agencies already receive rather than new mandates without funding, and the bill reserves grants for small and rural departments, which softens the burden. The data collection is the mechanism that makes the ban enforceable in practice — without it, profiling claims are hard to prove.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the Senate Judiciary Committee from May 2013 onward; a Judiciary subcommittee held a hearing on it in December 2014, but the full committee never acted and the Senate never voted before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Benjamin Cardin introduced the bill on May 23, 2013 with 18 Democratic cosponsors, all in the Senate, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary.
The Judiciary Subcommittee on the Constitution, Civil Rights and Human Rights held a hearing on the bill on December 9, 2014 — the only committee action in the bill's entire lifespan.
The full Judiciary Committee never reported the bill, and it never received a floor vote in either chamber before the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Law enforcement agencies avoided new profiling prohibitions, mandatory stop data collection, grant conditions, and potential lawsuits; communities affected by profiling were left with the status quo.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Law enforcement agencies; no new profiling rules

for.name: Sen. Benjamin Cardin
for.role: U.S. Senator from Maryland; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the End Racial Profiling Act of 2013 on May 23, 2013 and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

for.role: Cosponsors, including Sens. Durbin, Blumenthal, Coons, Harkin, Menendez, Stabenow, Levin, Mikulski, Warren, Boxer, Gillibrand, Lautenberg, and Hirono

for.name: Sen. Richard Durbin
for.role: Chair, Senate Judiciary Subcommittee on the Constitution, Civil Rights and Human Rights
for.what_they_did: Held the bill's only committee action, a subcommittee hearing on December 9, 2014.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee leadership
against.role: Full committee chair and majority, 113th Congress
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a committee markup or reported the bill in the roughly 19 months after referral, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress; the subcommittee hearing in December 2014 came near the session's close and was not followed by committee action.

sides.party_line_note: All 19 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican signed on; the bill never reached a vote, so no recorded opposition tally exists.

industries.industry: Law enforcement agencies (federal, state, local, and tribal police departments)
industries.note: The bill would require agencies to ban profiling, retrain officers, collect and report data on every stop and search, and open complaint procedures, with grant money at stake for noncompliance and lawsuits available against agencies, officers, and their supervisors. Agencies' interest in avoiding these costs and legal exposure ran against the communities the bill was written to protect.

industries.industry: Federal justice grant recipients (state and local governments receiving Byrne and COPS funding)
industries.note: Grant recipients would face certification requirements and possible withholding of Byrne Memorial and COPS funds, but could also compete for new federal grants to build data systems and training programs, with a reserved share for small and rural agencies. The conditionality uses money they already receive, so the net is new strings attached to existing funding.

The profiling definition covers immigration and customs enforcement, including enhanced entry inspections and workplace investigations, restricting reliance on national origin and religion in those operations — an area where agencies have traditionally claimed operational discretion.
